subject: R package on a Mac for lat lon data to look at spatial sympatry across a geographic range

messages.author: 46bb6905ac398c42
messages.subject: R package on a Mac for lat lon data to look at spatial sympatry across a geographic range
parts:
I am also working on predicting parasite host range using functional traits such as spatial sympatry, temporal phenology, and chemical congruency.   I was wondering if there is an R program that could take lat lon decimal data to cluster map different host spatial distribution compared with the parasite.  This parasite switches to different hosts across its geographic range from southern CA, to OR and into UT, NV and AZ.  I know I can just map the GPS points of the hosts, but wondered if something like argosfilter could be adapted for such a use.  Environmental filtering sorts out the phenological synchrony.  I think I am looking for a package that could take lat lon decimal data and visualize it as a 2D cluster image (which is similar to a map!:))  I could also use help with MDS analysis of chemical data. 

Leslie

messages.subject: Re: [D-RUG]: R package on a Mac for lat lon data to look at spatial sympatry across a geographic range
parts:
Hey Leslie,

Not sure if I totally follow what you are looking for, but here is one way to create such a visualization, using the package 'igraph'. 
library(raster)
library(igraph)
library(maps)
 
set.seed(111)
# Generate random sample of data points in lon lat
x <- sample( seq(-110, -114, length.out = 2000), 20)
y <- sample( seq( 36.98, 42, length.out = 2000),20)
id <- 1:20
map('state','utah')
text(x,y,id)
 
# generate distance matrix (in meters)
pd <- pointDistance( cbind(x,y), lonlat = TRUE, allpairs = TRUE) 
 
# make symmetrical and inverse (large distances = weaker connection)
pd[upper.tri(pd)] <- t(pd)[upper.tri(pd)]
pd <- 1/ pd
 
# transform to a complete 'graph' (vertex = point, edge = distance)
g <- graph.adjacency(pd, weighted =TRUE, diag = FALSE, mode = 'undirected') 
 
# here is a simple way visualize joint proximities, by deleting all connections above a certain distance (here, arbitrarily, the 50th percentile of all distances)
g2 <- delete.edges(g, which(E(g)$weight < quantile(E(g)$weight, .5)))
plot(g2)
 
# There are many other ways to detect clusters/communities among the network and visualize them, e.g.: 
fg <- fastgreedy.community(g)
h <- hclust(fg); plot(h)
